text:
An interval needs just two numbers: an estimate, and its standard error. Fifty users spend an average of forty-nine dollars twenty-eight a month. That's the estimate. Another fifty would average something else, and the standard error says by how much: about a dollar fifty. Multiply it by a critical value, two point oh one, and you get the margin of error: three dollars and six cents. Step that far either way, and the interval runs from forty-six twenty-two to fifty-two thirty-three. Why not the usual one point nine six? The spread was estimated from the same fifty people, and the t-distribution widens the band a little to pay for that. Building one is easy. Saying what it means is where people slip.

So play god for a moment. Here's a population whose true mean you know: a hundred. Draw forty values, build an interval... then do it again, a hundred times. Ninety-four intervals catch the true mean. Six miss it. The misses used the same correct recipe. They just drew unlucky samples. So the ninety-five percent describes the recipe: run it again and again, and about ninety-five in a hundred catch the truth. Your interval is just ONE of these lines. It holds the truth or it doesn't... and you can't see which. That's the sentence almost everyone gets wrong.

The usual version: there's a ninety-five percent chance the true mean is in this interval. But the true mean never moves. Once your interval is drawn, nothing is random any more. It's in, or it's out. Another misreading: ninety-five percent of the data falls inside. Back to the fifty users. Only eleven of the fifty spend inside it. The interval pins down their average, not any one person. And a wider interval isn't safer. It's just less precise.
